opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those distinctions that sounds pedantic at first but turns out to be the heart of the matter.

The population loss is the loss you'd get if you could average over the true data distribution, every possible input the world could throw at your model, weighted by how likely it is. It's a deterministic function on parameter space. It doesn't depend on which particular dataset you happened to draw. The empirical loss is what you actually compute in training: the average loss over your finite sample of n data points. It's a random function, because a different draw of data gives you a slightly different landscape.

Generalization is about the gap between those two. You train on the empirical loss, but what you care about is the population loss. The question is when minimizing the one gets you close to minimizing the other.

What singular learning theory tells you is that the answer is controlled by the geometry of the population loss near its minima. As n grows, the empirical loss converges to the population loss, and the fluctuations around it shrink in a precise way. So the structure that persists, the thing that matters asymptotically, is the shape of the set of true parameters and how the population loss rises as you move away from it.

In classical regular models that shape is a nice quadratic bowl, and the answer is governed by the number of parameters. That's where intuitions like BIC and "d over 2 log n" come from. But neural networks are singular. The set of minimizers isn't an isolated point; it's an extended, often very degenerate set, and the loss can be extremely flat in many directions. The relevant measure of complexity then isn't the parameter count but the local learning coefficient, which captures how much volume of near-optimal parameters there is, essentially how degenerate the geometry is.

So when I say geometry governs generalization, I mean the geometry of the population loss. The empirical loss is the noisy shadow you actually get to see, and the theory explains how the Bayesian posterior and, we think, training dynamics, are drawn toward regions where that underlying population geometry is most degenerate, which are the solutions that generalize well. It also means you can estimate things like the learning coefficient from the empirical loss, which is what makes it practical for interpretability work: you're using the observable landscape to infer the structure of the one that really matters.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the population loss, defined over the true distribution, from the empirical loss actually computed on a finite sample.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says generalization is governed by the geometry of the population loss near its minima.

r003.rationale: It describes empirical loss as a random sample-based landscape that converges toward population loss, with shrinking fluctuations, and calls it a noisy shadow of the underlying population geometry.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the distinction is actually at the heart of how singular learning theory thinks about generalization, so it's worth being careful about it.

The population loss is the thing you actually care about but can never compute. It's the expected loss over the true data-generating distribution, the loss you'd get if you had infinite data. Think of it as a function on parameter space: for every setting of the weights, there's a number telling you how badly that network does on the distribution as a whole. That function has a geometry. It has minima, it has valleys, it has these degenerate regions where many different parameters give the same loss. And crucially, that geometry is fixed. It doesn't depend on which dataset you happened to sample.

The empirical loss is what you can compute. It's the average loss on your particular finite sample of n data points. It's also a function on parameter space, and for large n it's a noisy approximation of the population loss. But the key word there is noisy. Every time you draw a different dataset, you get a slightly different empirical loss landscape. So the empirical loss is really a random function, and the population loss is what it's fluctuating around.

Now, why does this matter for generalization? Because training sees the empirical loss, but generalization is about the population loss. The gap between them is exactly what generalization error is. And the thing singular learning theory tells you, which I think is genuinely surprising, is that the size of that gap isn't controlled by the number of parameters in the usual way. It's controlled by the local geometry of the population loss near the minimum, specifically by this quantity called the learning coefficient, which measures how degenerate or how flat the loss is in a particular, precise sense.

So if you're in a region where the population loss is very degenerate, meaning there's a large volume of parameters that all achieve nearly the same loss, the empirical loss fluctuations matter less. The noise in your finite sample can't push you very far in terms of population loss, because the landscape is flat in those directions. The learning coefficient captures that, and it's what shows up in the asymptotic expansion of the Bayesian free energy, taking the role that parameter count plays in the classical regular case.

The subtlety people sometimes miss is that you have to be talking about the population loss when you define that geometry. If you compute the Hessian of the empirical loss at a minimum, you're looking at something contaminated by sampling noise, and the degeneracies you see may or may not reflect the true structure. The geometry that governs generalization is the geometry of the thing you can't see, and the empirical loss is your window onto it.

r001.rationale: The response says population loss is “the thing you actually care about but can never compute.”

r002.rationale: It identifies population-loss geometry as the geometry governing generalization and says the learning coefficient captures its effect.

r003.rationale: It describes empirical loss as a noisy sample-based approximation and explains how population-loss degeneracy affects the impact of empirical fluctuations.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is that population loss is an expectation over the true data distribution, whereas empirical loss is an average over the finite sample you actually have. So empirical loss is what you can compute and optimize, but population loss is what you ultimately care about: how well does the model perform on fresh data?

And each of those defines a function on parameter space, so each has a geometry. They're related, but they aren't identical. With a finite sample, you can have directions in parameter space along which the empirical loss barely changes, even though the population loss does change. So fitting the training data doesn't, by itself, tell you where you are in the population landscape.

From the perspective of singular learning theory, what's particularly interesting is the geometry near the set of parameters that minimize population loss. That set needn't be an isolated point with a nice quadratic bowl around it. It can have intersecting components, degeneracies, and directions in which parameters aren't identifiable. That local structure helps govern the statistical relationship between training loss and generalization loss. So the geometry that matters isn't simply how sharp a minimum looks in the training landscape; it's how the model's population geometry interacts with finite sampling.

r001.rationale: It contrasts population loss as an expectation over the true distribution with empirical loss as the finite-sample quantity that can be computed and optimized, conveying that population loss is not directly accessible.

r002.rationale: It says the local structure of population-loss minima helps govern the relationship between training loss and generalization, and that population geometry interacts with finite sampling.

r003.rationale: It describes how population and empirical landscapes can differ along parameter directions and says population geometry interacts with finite sampling, communicating that population geometry relates to sample-based empirical loss behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
The empirical loss is the loss you calculate on the finite training set, whereas the population loss is the expected loss on the underlying distribution that generated the data. So empirical loss is what you can measure and optimize, and population loss is what you ultimately care about when you ask whether the model generalizes.

Geometrically, these are two different functions on the same parameter space. The training sample makes the empirical loss a random function, while the population loss describes the underlying landscape. The important question is how the region selected by training sits within that population landscape. Having a small empirical loss doesn’t, by itself, tell you that the population loss is small.

In singular learning theory, we’re particularly interested in the geometry near sets of parameters that represent the same distribution. Those sets can have intersections and degeneracies, so the geometry isn’t adequately described by an isolated minimum with a positive-definite Hessian. That local structure helps determine how finite-sample learning translates into generalization.

r001.rationale: It contrasts empirical loss as what can be measured and optimized with population loss as the underlying distribution’s landscape, conveying that the latter is not directly accessible in practice.

r002.rationale: It says local structure helps connect finite-sample learning to generalization, but does not clearly identify the geometry of the population loss itself as the geometry that mathematically governs generalization.

r003.rationale: It says sampling makes empirical loss a random function, but does not state that population-loss geometry influences the behavior of empirical losses computed from samples.
